speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the problem of airport noise from Pearson airport is very real and continues unabated.
The airport's surrounding communities have had to endure frequent aircraft take-off and landings every 30 seconds in late night flights on the routes directly over their homes well past the established airport's curfew.
During my meetings with the numerous community and ratepayer groups along with hundreds of local residents in my riding, they demand that the Minister of Transport enforce the regulations at least to alternate flights to and from Pearson on runways 24R and 24L.
In addition, the cavalier attitude expressed by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport against community groups is offensive to their concerns and displays his lack of understanding of the problem at hand. His misguided comments in the Mississauga news, for example, show blatant disregard for the plight of the public.
The minister and government must act now so that the pleas of community groups living around Pearson are not drowned out by airport noise or any noise emanating from the government benches.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. Marcel Danis, the Minister of Labour and
member for Vercheres, who managed to include an amendment to section 7 in the special back-to-work legislation for postal workers.
Thanks to this amendment, postal workers were able to have the legislation cover certain items on which agreement had been reached during the mediation process under Judge Alan Gold.
Mr. Danis did this to ensure that what had already been accomplished during the process would not be lost.

Mr. Speaker, today the Minister of National Defence announced that the government was consenting to all future visits to Canada of U.S. and U.K. nuclear powered and nuclear armed military vessels.
This decision is taken without any public participation or consultation. In fact by using the Order in Council route, a procedure already ruled illegal by the Canadian courts, the government is deliberately seeking to avoid a public environmental review.
The consequences of a nuclear accident, especially in built-up areas such as Victoria, are incredibly serious. Emergency procedures are not fully in place.
Finally the decision flies in face of the rapid de-escalation of the nuclear arms race. Instead of taking this particular position the government should have shown leadership and placed a moratorium on nuclear visits to Canadian waters at least until a full public independent environmental assessment takes place.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many church congregations throughout my constituency of Brandon-Souris are actively participating in White

October 30, 1991
Ribbons Against Pornography Week, October 27 to November 3.
I would like to take this opportunity to add my words of support to this campaign. In an age of increasing violence, which seems to be particularly and tragically directed against women and children, society must do all it can to negate the all too present message which erroneously suggests to some that such violence is an inevitable part of life.
Society must also address the problem of the production and utilization of pornographic materials, and particularly when children are the subjects. Such degrading and exploitive material by implication diminishes the values of those who are portrayed therein and in my opinion helps create a climate which leads directly to the violence which we abhor, to the violence which must be prevented.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade tabled a document in this House entitled Prosperity Through Competitiveness.
He started out his comments by saying "Canadians today are perplexed and confused". That was the most meaningful statement of his entire speech. He went on to talk about prosperity, education and other subjects. He did not mention the fact that because of the government's softwood lumber tax which was belatedly removed and the high Canadian dollar this government has been guilty of increasing welfare payments by 500 per cent to 2,000 per cent in some municipalities where lumber was the main industrial employer.
He forgot to tell this House that when he was Minister of Finance the transfer payments to the provinces for education were cut back. Training programs were cut back. He forgot to tell Canadians that his government promised large increases in research and development to help Canada to be more competitive. Today research and development is at its lowest point in decades.
Because of what the government has failed to do, it has created havoc and hardship for many families and
has discouraged young people in their outlook for the future. It has failed the children and young people of this nation and it has failed the very nation itself.

Mr. Speaker, it is with pride that I rise today to share the news of an important honour bestowed upon one of our members.
Last week the Canadian National Institute for the Blind and the Louis Braille Memorial Committee awarded the Louis Braille commemorative medallion to the hon. Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship.
It is a rare honour, having been presented to Canadian recipients only on two previous occasions since 1952 when the medallion was first struck in Paris. The distinguished award was given at the launch of the Braille Literacy Foundation in Toronto. The Government of Canada has placed $1 million toward the establishment of this vital and high profile project. This contribution is but the most recent of numerous steps forward that we have taken in the area of literacy, in partnership with business, labour, various levels of government and the voluntary sector.
The silver medallion was presented to our minister and is indeed a shining tribute to the universality of literacy in our land.

Mr. Speaker, the time for this government to act in the interests of Canadian women who have had the Meme breast implant has long passed. We have heard the words of concern from the present minister and the pious assertions of his predecessors that all was being done to safeguard the health of Canadian women.
What we have yet to see is any concrete action to address this serious health issue.
Following my meeting with the minister in July, we were assured that an internal review of his department, and the approval that followed of the Meme breast implant for use in Canada, was under way and would be available soon. We are still waiting.
October 30, 1991

I have asked the minister in this House and in other forums to establish an independent judicial inquiry into the actions taken by his department in allowing the Meme to be sold in Canada.
Today I request on behalf of the thousands of Canadian women who have had the Meme breast implant the establishment of an independent external audit of the working of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
In particular the actions taken or omitted by the Medical Devices Branch of that department need to be the subject of a comprehensive investigation. Canadian women have the right to know the exact extent to which this government has gone to safeguard their health.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Youth); Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for more than 25 years, the best pee-wee hockey players have met annually to play during a ten-day tournament in the riding of Quebec-Est.
This international event is absolutely unique. For more than 25 years, the tournament has received nothing but praise from heads of State, hockey organizations, and especially from parents and participants.
Many great hockey players consider this an unforgettable experience. We have never heard any remarks with racist overtones, when we welcome hundreds of native people, Europeans and Asians.
I must say, however, that with Max Gros-Louis, I deplore the negative overtones of an exchange between Bev Morin and the president of the tournament. I am sure it was an unfortunate misunderstanding, and I am convinced that no one wants to use young people for political purposes.
In February 1992, Quebec-Est will once again welcome thousands of young people who will come here to have fun, demonstrate their skills and get to know each
other. We hope the team from Thompson will be applauded just like other participating teams.

Mr. Speaker, over one million children in Canada are living in poverty, too many of them deprived of the basic human rights of adequate food, shelter and clothing.
In response to concerns raised here by me and across this country by others, it is obvious that the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare have never been forced to deny their own children food when they were hungry, drink when they were thirsty, adequate shelter when they were homeless, a loving home because economic stress had caused familial breakdown and havoc. Not having experienced this themselves, they deny the harsh reality of it for other Canadians.
The consequences of raising over one million children in Canada in conditions of poverty will be more devastating to our nation's well-being than our current debt. Our children are our nation's future. More than enough studies indicate how impoverished children become the health, illiteracy, early school dropout, disabled and welfare statistics of the future. This government must get real, re-evaluate current policies and assure that all future policies set the well-being of our nation's children as its first priority.

Mr. Speaker, less than 4 per cent of Canadians live on farms today, yet the industry generates billions of dollars worth of exports each year. In fact, from 1969 to 1988 the value of agricultural exports grew from $1.2 billion to $10.3 billion.
However, in recent years our farm industry across Canada has been devastated by record low prices for their quality products. In the midst of this crisis in agriculture, Canadians continue to pay the world's second lowest percentage of disposable income on food.

October 30,1991
Oral Questions
I think it is time that Canadians consider providing recognition and long-term support for our food producers by paying a targeted levy on the over $40 billion we spend each year on food. For example, the levy could be an annually adjusted rate which is designed to ensure a minimum farm income equal to a pre-1990 five-year average.
If our pledges of support for the family farm are to be more than just empty rhetoric, then we as Canadians should be willing to pay a small premium on our food bill to ensure the survival of agriculture, which historically has meant so much to our national economy.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today to draw the attention of this House once again to a situation in the riding of Beausejour that is most unfair. In most of New Brunswick, workers need ten weeks of unemployment to be eligible for unemployment insurance programs. In Westmorland, however, the requirement is sixteen weeks, which for some people is out of the question.

A big proportion of workers in Westmorland will not find the required 16 weeks of work. I ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration to make the necessary adjustments so that the people of rural Westmorland will be treated exactly the same way as the people of rural Kent who are treated differently.
I want to see everybody treated the same way. That is why I am asking the minister to treat all the fishermen and workers of the riding of Beausejour with justice.

Mr. Speaker, today marks the 19th anniversary of the class of 1972, those members of Parliament first elected on October 30, 1972 who went on to unbroken re-election victories and still sit as members of this House. I believe these members deserve to be recognized as the rare breed they are: political survivors.
On October 30, 1972, 59 Conservatives, 23 Liberals, 11 New Democrats, and 3 Socreds were elected for the first time. Mr. Speaker, I am proud to say that you and I were counted among those numbers. However, of the 96 there are only 11 Conservatives and 2 Liberals remaining with unbroken electoral records.
In the Liberal caucus there remain Jean-Robert Gauthier and the Hon. Bill Rompkey. In the Conservative caucus there is you, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Harvie Andre, the Hon. Perrin Beatty, the Right Hon. Joe Clark, the Hon. Paul Dick, the Hon. Jake Epp, the Hon. Otto Jelinek, Bill Kempling, Gus Mitges, the Hon. Frank Oberle, and myself.
In an age when public cynicism is high and the fortunes of political life at an all-time low, we are to be commended for our resiliency and ability to buck the trend.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Today the Secretary of State for External Affairs again gave in to pressure from the Americans. By order in council, she gave them the right of passage for their nuclear-powered submarines in Canadian territorial waters.
Mr. Speaker, can the Prime Minister tell us why the government again yielded to American pressure, when the cold war is over?
Does the government intend to rescind this utterly ridiculous order in council?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the matter of sovereignty over Canadian territorial waters is clear. We agreed to the situation involving submarines and we continue to consult the Americans, but it was done cooperatively.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Prime Minister.
October 30,1991

Oral Questions
It is not the first time that this government has failed to defend the sovereignty of Canada. It seems to me that every time President Bush sneezes the Prime Minister catches pneumonia.
When will the Prime Minister stop caving in to the President of the United States and start standing for Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allowing U.S. and British submarines into Canadian waters has been a part of Canadian defence policy for a great many years. This was done on a consultative basis. We have not in any way given up our sovereignty on the waters that are under dispute. It is clear to us that those are our waters. The Americans consulted with us. The submarines are coming with our consent and we have been able to achieve certain guarantees as a result of those discussions.
Now that is exercising sovereignty.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to know from the minister what kind of deal it is. We have said clearly for generations that we did not want any nuclear submarines in Canadian waters. Is it quid pro quo in order to have certain a concession, to accept that? We do not want these submarines in Canadian waters at all. It is clear; and this has been the position taken by this Parliament many times over.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as usual the Leader of the Opposition is totally on the wrong track. This is a part of our co-operative defence. It has been a part of our co-operative defence for a great many years and it will continue to be into the future.
I should point out that this is an acoustical testing facility only. It is not in any way a base for nuclear submarines. We are continuing to co-operate and we are realistic about our defence needs, about our deterrent needs and about our sovereignty, and that is what this is about.

Mr. Speaker, the government's decision has put our environment at risk. It has put at risk the lives of people. All the ports will now have warships visiting them. It thoroughly undermines our sovereignty, and it was done without any parliamentary debate, without any consultation with the people affected. It was done in secret.
How can this government claim there is any democracy left in Canada when it makes a decision like this that affects thousands of people and it is done behind closed doors?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Masse (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member seems to forget that in August 1967, long before Mr. Bush even thought of becoming President of the United States, we had a Liberal government in Canada which adopted a policy of allowing nuclear-powered ships to enter our territorial waters provided Canada had a verification procedure with the country concerned.
So this is not a new policy as the hon. member would have the House believe. Your government authorized such things in 1967!

Mr. Speaker, we have a minister who says: "If you let a thief in your house and you say 'surrender', somehow you have won a victory, and it is not a crime".
I want to ask the minister this. The Order in Council explicitly says as follows; "if claims arise out of a nuclear accident, there will be a diplomatic conference". Are we saying that we are going to have a diplomatic international conference over the ashes of people if there is a nuclear accident? Is that the safeguard this government has provided?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Masse (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that the hon. member should go back and see in his own notes what he would have done in 1968 in such a case, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Today the Economic Council of Canada has confirmed that the economic and budgetary policies of this government have set us on the road to the most costly and least desirable constitutional options, and I quote: "The government's decision to alter its commitments to existing fiscal arrangements with the provinces unleashed pressures for decentralization".

October 30, 1991
Oral Questions
I want to say to the Prime Minister that the most valued contribution he can make to unity in this country is to abandon the disastrous economic policies that have led to pressures for greater decentralization.
Therefore, I ask the Prime Minister, in the interests of turning the constitutional debate around in a direction that makes sense for all Canadians, will he immediately restore federal funding to health programs, post-secondary programs and social assistance so that we can deal with the needs of all Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, I have not had the opportunity to read carefully the document of the Economic Council of Canada to which my hon. friend refers. Apparently the principal conclusion is in regard to some economic consequences for sovereignty association.
That may have been an interesting conclusion when the question of sovereignty association was debated 11 years ago, and resolved 11 years ago. Sovereignty association is no longer relevant.
Oh, oh.
Apart from a few people who want to freeload on the back of Canada, I am telling you it is not an option.
Hear, hear.
I have a little message for them. You cannot be a part-time Canadian. You cannot have the benefits of Canada while you are trying to undermine the integrity of the nation on the other.
Hear, hear.

In Montreal last week I indicated that the question was one of great simplicity. You are either going to be a Canadian or you are going to be citizens of another country. Therefore, the Economic Council of Canada report might have been interesting 11 years ago, as it dealt with sovereignty association, the question that was on the ballot then.
The question now, for all of us to decide, is do you want one country Canada or do you want to be citizens of
a foreign country? When that question is squarely put to Quebecers, they will opt for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask a supplementary question. I agree with the Prime Minister 'that we must have a united Canada, but it is also a question of the government's economic policies. I would call the Prime Minister's attention to page 101, where it says that clearly, the present constitutional crisis is exacerbated by a whole series of financial and economic pressures. For example, the fight against inflation has produced very high unemployment.
So if the Prime Minister wants to build a Canada where everyone would like to live, will he put forward a recovery plan so that Quebec's 400,000 jobless can find work before the referendum, not after?

Mr. Speaker, I am told that this study concludes that sovereignty-association would cost each Quebec family at least $1,800 a year for at least a generation. That is sovereignty-association. The Council did not study the real issue, which is the cost of independence. If the Council concluded that sovereignty-association would cost $1,800 per Quebec family for a generation, imagine the cost of independence!

A supplementary, Mr. Speaker. I suggest to the Prime Minister that in this report there were very condemning conclusions about the economic policies of this government and the implications of that for national unity. Yes, sovereignty association was one subject. It was not the total of the report. It was the economic policies of this government.
For example, the report says the experience of the past two years should not be allowed to repeat itself. We on this side agree. Economic policies that caused unemployment cannot continue in this country.
I want to ask the Prime Minister again: Will his government immediately restore federal funding to such programs as health and social spending and post-secondary education? Will he do that now in the interest of national unity?
October 30,1991

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, while not having had an opportunity to study the report in detail, there is one thing that was drawn to my attention. That is the fact that the Economic Council is projecting real growth to reach 4.2 per cent in 1992 and 5.1 per cent in 1993. That compares with our projections of 3.2 per cent in 1992 and
4.1	per cent in 1993. They are considerably more optimistic on the growth front than we are. They are also more optimistic on the employment opportunities as well.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that clearly indicates that we are following a course of sustained durable recovery with price stability.
I am really surprised that the hon. member is so much against inflation. I thought that the NDP were the champions of the under dog, the senior citizens, the people on fixed incomes. It is runaway inflation that erodes the income base of senior citizens and low income people. They should be applauding our efforts.
With respect to transfer payments, when this government came into office, it transferred to the provinces in 1984-85 $25.6 billion. In 1992-93, in the next fiscal year, we will be transferring $38.1 billion, an increase of $12.5 billion or almost 50 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Yesterday the government launched its so-called prosperity and learning initiative in the House of Commons. Two ministers stood in the House and briefed Parliament and subsequently briefed the press in a press conference and answered questions about the reported $15 million program.
I want to ask the Prime Minister this. Why did both those ministers, the minister of trade and the minister of employment, withhold information about an additional $4.5 million advertising program to be jointly funded by both their ministries, 50-50, and to be launched in the next few weeks, and an advertising blitz called "Yes We Can"? Why were Canadians not given all the information yesterday?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe at that press conference and certainly on other occasions yesterday I talked quite openly about advertising. I did say that there would be an advertising program. It would be financed in part from the secretariat, $500,000 from the secretariat, but in part from the budgets of other government departments.
It is those other government departments which have other advertising programs in government and will be doing so under the broad umbrella of the "Yes We Can" theme, the competitiveness theme.
It is not incremental spending in that sense. I have been quite open about it and I will continue to be open about it.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians should note that the program has grown from $15 million to $20 million in 24 hours.
I want to ask the minister another question. It was clear yesterday in the briefing with the senior official involved, Mr. Tony Eyton, that an unspecified amount of money is also going to be spent on consultants and to pay for studies.
The estimate given yesterday was $5 million for that program. Will the minister now confirm that yesterday's initiative is not $15 million, but with the $5 million he just admitted and with another $5 million in his new spirit of openness-I expect him to admit this-the total program is $25 million.
Rather than listening to Canadians, $15 million is going to be spent on a communications and advertising blitz. How can you say you are listening when you are dumping a barrage of propaganda on the heads of Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I think my hon. friend was told this morning by members of the secretariat that $5 million which he has just concluded now is going to be an advertising blitz is nothing like an advertising blitz.
It is moneys that will be spent on consultants, on printing and distribution, toll free telephone information services and things that are related to serving the consultation process on a community basis.

October 30, 1991
Oral Questions
If the hon. member wants to ask me another question, he can ask the other question.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 9, 1980, the then Leader of the Opposition, the right hon. member for Yellowhead said about advertising: "I think that attempts to spend public money to manipulate public opinion on public questions that have not been decided is an improper practice that offends the right of the House of Commons".
I want to ask the minister who has just answered how he can justify spending $25 million that Canadians do not have to propagate the policy of a failing government. How can that be right?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is suggesting that we should not be talking about the challenges of international competitiveness.
He is suggesting that these are not issues that Canadians want to learn more about and that Canadians do want to participate in in a broad way as we are proposing through the community consultations.
I would tell my hon. friend first of all that Canadians want to participate in them. They have said that international competitiveness is the most important issue that they are facing in a poll that was put out just on Monday by the Toronto Star and the CBC.
We are responding to that great concern by watching this prosperity initiative so we can strengthen the economy of this country in the coming years.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to remind the minister that the ultimate democratic consultation is called an election.

My supplementary is directed to the Prime Minister, the ultimate guardian of the public purse. Once more, Tory cronies are going to dip into it and receive advertising contracts. Will the Prime Minister make a commitment today and promise all Canadians that none of this money will be spent before there is a public tender for advertising contracts? Is he prepared to give us this assurance today?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have indicated our proposal to launch the broadest possible consultation process.
A large amount of the spending that is in that money that was referred to by his colleague is money that is being spent within the government on public servants who are being reallocated from other government departments.
To suggest that this is a total amount of new money first of all is wrong. It is reallocated money. It is reallocated people directed to focus on the most important economic issue that we are facing today, improving our competitive position internationally.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Despite the distortions and protests of the Liberals earlier in Question Period, it was in fact they who opened our territorial waters and ports to nuclear vessels a quarter of a century ago.
Shameful.

What has happened today to the Dixon Entrance, the richest fishing grounds in Canada, is however much more serious. It is on those points that I would like the Secretary of State to address her mind. The technique that has been used to exempt U.S. nuclear submarines from transiting Dixon Entrance was found to be illegal by the Federal Court in May of this year.
My question to the minister is this: Why has she and the cabinet chosen to use a technique that has already been found illegal and denies the public in British Columbia the right to assess the real and measurable risks of submarines involved in testing activities in our waters and to the north of our waters?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, let me remind the hon. member of two things. First of all, this is an acoustical testing facility. It is not a nuclear testing facility.
Second, let me remind the hon. member that the history of U.S. nuclear submarines is an excellent one in terms of safety, that we have discussed with them and we have consent from them concerning their use of our sovereign waters and that we have received from them
October 30, 1991

assurances on how these waters will be passed through by these submarines to reach the acoustic testing facility.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is to the same minister because this is much more serious than what the minister wants to address. Certainly a public review is where you address the serious risks that the public face.
What I am asking is a procedural question of the minister. It is abundantly clear from documentation that was provided to cabinet that this technique was already found to be illegal in the Kemano-Alcan case. You cannot use Order in Council powers to exempt yourself in any decision from things such as this.
My question to the minister is will you remove yourself from this situation-
The matter the hon. member raises is of course important, but I do ask hon. members to stay within the rules in presenting their questions.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think there are two important things here. First of all, the environmental aspects of this activity were reviewed pursuant to the 1990 cabinet decision to ascertain the environmental implications of cabinet decisions.
Responsible departments did analyse the information that was relevant to this activity including the final environmental impact statement assessment, as was done for the SEAFAC facility, the thoroughness of which has successfully withstood a court challenge in the U.S.
Pursuant to government policy, the results of a preliminary environmental assessment will be made available to the public.

subtopic: CONVENTION ON THE RIGHTS OF THE CHILD
CONVENTION ON THE RIGHTS OF THE CHILD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, over a year ago, the Prime Minister co-chaired with great fanfare the United Nations World Summit for Children where the Convention on the Rights of the Child was passed. This convention still sits on the shelf in the Prime Minister's office gathering dust.

subtopic: CONVENTION ON THE RIGHTS OF THE CHILD
speechtext:
You are all wrong.
Oral Questions

subtopic: CONVENTION ON THE RIGHTS OF THE CHILD
speechtext: Fine. Will the Prime Minister today then, if I am so absolutely wrong, do the right thing and send a message to all Canadian children and to the advocates who are sitting here in the House and tell them where, when and how this convention will be signed?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CONVENTION ON THE RIGHTS OF THE CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the convention is not on the shelf of the Prime Minister. The convention has been proposed to the provinces as we said it would. The provinces are first responsible for children.
What the Prime Minister and I said is that as soon as the provinces have ratified or accepted the convention, it will be signed. We are still waiting for two provinces, one of which was recently involved in an election, and we are told that the provinces will deal quickly with the matter. I still say that the convention will be ratified before the end of the year.

subtopic: CONVENTION ON THE RIGHTS OF THE CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the minister knows when the convention is going to be passed then political will should get it passed now.
The plight of the children of Canada is really staggering. One in six live in poverty, homelessness is at emergency levels, too many children still live in families that live below the poverty line, health conditions for our aboriginal children compare to that of the Third World, and this government's economic mismanagement is driving more people on to the bread lines.
My question to the Prime Minister is this. What concrete steps is he taking that will address and redress, right now, the crisis conditions faced by over one million Canadian children who are still living in poverty in this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CONVENTION ON THE RIGHTS OF THE CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will answer right now. This week I had four meetings with people dealing with children. I do not believe there is one member in this House who does not want to deal with the problems of children. It is a very serious one and must be addressed by all Canadians.
The member will recall that all departments of this government spend approximately $15 billion a year. We would like to do more and we will. I have already announced that the government will come forward with

October 30,1991
Oral Questions
a strategy before the end of the year. We will need the help of every Canadian.
I believe that Canadians understand that to be able to provide services to children we have to create the resources. I ask my friend to help me get the resources, starting with a good economy in this country.

subtopic: CONVENTION ON THE RIGHTS OF THE CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in times of economic distress, children must be the last to suffer.
A year ago the Prime Minister said at the UN World Summit for Children: "Canada still has serious problems that affect children in many ways".
This morning on Parliament Hill, some 500 child symposium delegates told members of Parliament: "Child poverty in Canada is a national scandal".
Since a national child care program is crucial to any child poverty strategy, when will this government make good on this age old promise?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CONVENTION ON THE RIGHTS OF THE CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of the hon. member I will repeat what I said to his predecessor. This government has a long-standing commitment to dealing with problems concerning children, not just daycare but also the whole problem of child sexual abuse, family violence and school drop-outs. I think this is a global problem.
So far, in terms of available resources, the government has gone as far as it could in allocating those resources, and it is committed to doing more in the future. But this cannot happen, Mr. Speaker -As I told the groups this morning, I refuse to make any promises because it all depends on our capacity to generate the necessary resources. And as I said before-since I was asked not to talk about interest rates-when interest rates are at 25 per cent, there are no available resources to take care of Canada's children.

subtopic: CONVENTION ON THE RIGHTS OF THE CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government knew its resources when it promised day care six years ago and several times since, but it did not fulfil the promise.
Another very sad fact is that aboriginal children in Canada live under horrific health and social standards, with an acutely high number of infant deaths and suicides.
What is the minister prepared to do today to eliminate these alarming problems? Will he allow Canada's children to become the lost generation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CONVENTION ON THE RIGHTS OF THE CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity last summer to visit many reserves in Canada, particularly in the member's home province.
I totally agree with him that what is a problem for white people becomes a more difficult problem for aboriginal people in all parts of the country. That is why the health services branch of the department is working closely with the chiefs of the First Nations.
I asked the ministers of health of all provinces to be with me at a meeting in Winnipeg last September with leaders of the aboriginal communities to find a way to answer the health problems of children in particular. We put particular emphasis on children. Once again, it has to be done within the capacity we have. I am looking forward to continuing to work with Indian leaders to give all the relief we can to aboriginal children in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
South Africa has made significant strides in dismantling apartheid and perhaps now is the time to reconsider having normal trading relations with that country. Therefore, my question is this: when will the government lift trade sanctions?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to report that, as a result of efforts by this government through working with the Commonwealth, the sanctions policy with regard to South Africa has proven to be an effective one.
As a result of the progress made in South Africa, the Commonwealth heads of government two weeks ago agreed to an immediate removal of people to people sanctions and indeed, Canada has already done that.
October 30,1991

The trade and investment sanctions will be lifted when there are appropriate transitional mechanisms agreed to by all the parties. It is our hope that there will be an all-party conference in the near future, but we do not want to prejudge at this point what those transitional arrangements might be.
We are pleased to see some progress. We are looking for more, and once those transitional arrangements are in place, we will be happy to take further steps as outlined in the Commonwealth report.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
As the minister responsible for children, I would like to ask the minister a very simple question. Does the minister agree with his colleague, the Minister for International Trade, who last week claimed that no man, woman or child goes without adequate medical care, decent shelter or proper food in Canada, or does he believe the over 500 delegates at the Canada's children conference who told him today that it is a national scandal that there are over one million children living in poverty in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would agree that as long as there is one child in this country having a problem with poverty or violence, there is a problem. I agree with that. I said that on Monday and I repeated it this morning. But the fact of the matter is, we have to find the answers. The answers have to be based upon the fact that we have the capacity to provide even more than $15 billion a year by all departments of this government.
But I call on my friend to help me to find a way. He knows very well when 250,000 people lose their jobs in Ontario, it means more poor people, more poor children. If we can give these people a chance to find jobs in a good economy, we give a chance to the children of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to hear that from the minister. Perhaps the next time he is sitting beside the Minister for
Oral Questions
International Trade in cabinet he could explain a few things to him and maybe we will see some solutions for Canada's children.
Later this year Canada will ratify the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. This convention commits Canada to recognizing "the right of every child to a standard of living adequate for the child's physical, mental, spiritual, moral and social development."
The government has capped social assistance contributions for over half of Canada's poor, deindexed critical social programs, cut back education, health funding and equalization payments and reneged on its commitment regarding child care.
I ask the minister if he can explain to us how these measures will fulfil the commitments this government has undertaken under the UN convention.

Mr. Speaker, I simply repeat the commitment I made at the United Nations, that we expect the convention to be ratified by the end of 1991. That is within this year. That was the undertaking I made on behalf of the Government of Canada and it will be respected.
One of the problems we have is to make sure it is accepted and implemented within areas of provincial jurisdiction. In Saskatchewan, for example, I believe we are still waiting for a response. I am sure that the new government, upon its swearing in, will deal with this on a priority basis. As soon as it signifies its intention to fully ratify the provisions that apply provincially, we will make certain the rest of it is done.
We view our commitment to children as an extremely high priority, not only for the government but for all members of the House. My hon. friend suggests that we have been cutting back. The Minister of Finance has just indicated, contrary to the contention, that transfer payments by the federal government to the provinces, transfers to children, to the elderly, to welfare and so on, have increased by 50 per cent in seven years. The total amount is some $12.5 billion.
I want to point out to my hon. friend, when he is talking about the problems of children, these are not because we have cut back-perhaps as a nation we haven't done enough-but we have increased dramati-

October 30,1991
Oral Questions
cally the contribution of this government to children; it is not because we have cut back.
We have increased funding, although as a nation obviously we have to do much more, and we will.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for either the Minister of National Revenue or the Minister of Finance.
It concerns the GST credit for 18 year olds. In the province of Alberta, and I assume all of Canada, an 18 year old is considered an adult. They can drive a car, they can go into debt, they can vote and they can pay taxes. However, they cannot collect the GST credit unless they are a parent or married.
Many young people are very independent by 18. They live on their own and try to make ends meet. The refusal to pay them the GST credit is a slap in the face, saying that they really aren't independent at all.
The quirk in this new goods and services tax is discriminatory based on age. Is the minister going to correct this quirk and allow all eligible 18 year olds to collect the GST credit?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the GST refund for people under the age of 19 is handled in exactly the same way as the federal sales tax refund was handled. To do what the hon. member suggests would be administratively very difficult if not impossible. As he knows, if they are claimed as a dependent living with their parents, they do qualify. If they are married and under the age of 19 they qualify for the GST rebate and if they have any children they qualify for that as well.
But I repeat, it would administratively difficult to alter the way in which it is being administered as it was under the FST.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs and it concerns the Canadian woman who has been held hostage in Lebanon for the last six years.
The minister said in a letter to me earlier this week that there is no proof that Mrs. Haddad was taken hostage. What about Lebanese press reports of her kidnapping on September 26, 1985? What about the four people who heard Nabih Berri, head of the Shi'ite militia, say his group was holding Mrs. Haddad? What about the three Lebanese hostages who said they saw Mrs. Haddad during their own captivity? And what about the medical doctor who was told she was held hostage?
How much proof does the Canadian government need before we will act on behalf of a Canadian citizen who has been held hostage for six years?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government has been very, very concerned about Mrs. Haddad and has undertaken exhaustive inquiries as to her safety and whereabouts both through sending diplomatic notes to the government and through direct inquiries with a number of organizations within Lebanon.
There is simply some question as to how and where. There is no question about her disappearance at all and there is no question that this is a tragedy for the family. When this first happened the department worked very hard to establish her whereabouts and to establish if and how she was actually taken hostage by a particular group. We have made exhaustive inquiries. We have worked through every possible diplomatic level to try and aid both Mrs. Haddad and her family here.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has not even put her on the international list of hostages.
Professor Humphrey, one of the world's leading scholars and for 20 years the director of the United Nations division of human rights, has called upon the Canadian government specifically to acknowledge that Mrs. Haddad is a hostage in Lebanon. I ask the minister to at least request the United Nations hostage negotiator to include her in the list of western hostages.
Will the minister ask that Mrs. Haddad be included in the list of western hostages?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are certain ways of dealing with this. The Canadian government has made inquiries and it has pursued this matter aggressively in every forum available to it. Immediately following the incident six years ago and recently, it is has been a continuing file, a file that is continually open for us in a
October 30, 1991

number of forums. We have also been in constant touch with the family.
I would like to be able to do more and we will continue to do everything we can. We are continuing to pursue this as a case that requires our very great sympathy, our concern and our action.

Mr. Speaker, at a time when 400,000 young Canadians are unemployed, the best this government can do is to offer the "Learning Well

Living Well" consultation paper asking Canadians for ideas.
The Economic Council made this observation in its annual report. I quote: "The problem of unemployment is cumulative. Young workers get trapped in a cycle of short-term, seasonal, insecure jobs and unemployment insurance dependencies and are unable to break away from it".
I ask the minister of employment this question. When is this government going to start learning well so that young Canadians can start living well?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the past two years we have defended and promoted in this House an employment strategy requiring intesified training. We have put in place partnership mechanisms with a view to achieving these objectives. Any delay that ensued must be blamed on the hon. member and members opposite who spent a whole year obstructing the passage of Bill C-21.
What we are trying to do with the programs we have, as quickly as possible, is give the requisite training to workers to prepare them for market globalization.

Mr. Speaker, if this government is serious about establishing a learning culture, then it must understand that education is a key
Oral Questions
component. In order for our young people to obtain an education, it must be accessible.
I ask the minister this question. Why has this government chosen to impose a 3 per cent tax on student loans? Why this attack on students who are in greatest need?

Mr. Speaker, I have answered this question time and time again in the House and I will repeat the same answer.

The review is under way with the provinces and we expect to be able to propose a document to this House in the next few months.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the minister responsible for ACOA and I think the acting minister is in the House. I hope it is the Minister of Public Works, who I know will be fully aware of the situation involving the Keddy's hotels and motor inns in Atlantic Canada. Over 1,000 to 1,200 direct employees at 11 motels will go down the drain.
Knowing the situation, knowing quite a bit of history of Keddy's, going back to the Hotel Nova Scotia in 1984-85, I am wondering if non-partisan, objective support from all sides would be a catalyst. Could the minister have his officials meet the Keddy's interests so that this situation will not end up in dire headlines, let alone the spin-off effect of all the other little industries that depend on this situation.

have spoken with colleagues. In all fairness I am not sure that at this stage, taking into account all of the circumstances, anything can be done.

Mr. Speaker, my questions is for the minister of corporate and consumer affairs.
Yesterday the minister responded to the recommendation of a floating cap on credit card interest rates by telling consumers to go out and negotiate a personal loan. In other words, you are not my concern. You are the bank's concern. Go and let the foxes get at you.
I want to ask this minister right now who he is looking out for: the corporations or the consumers? Why is the minister continuing to be an apologist for corporations and not a defender of the interests of the consumers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am surprised. I am not alone in saying that putting a cap on that is not acceptable. Even the Consumers' Association of Canada is on side with that. It does not think it is the solution.

I would say, Mr. Speaker, that it is especially important then to make the consumers aware of the fact that the credit card market is highly competitive. My colleague knows how committed I am to consumers, we were talking about this just last week.
You can go to your banker-something I would encourage everyone to do, as I said yesterday-who offers both credit cards and personal loans. Instead of buying goods on credit cards issued by department stores and other companies which charge interest rate between 19 and 28 per cent, consumers should take out a personal loan at 11 or 12 per cent, Mr. Speaker. I think we should
first increase consumers' awareness because we brought interest rates down to 8.5 per cent for their benefit. Consumers should take advantage of it.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Prime Minister.
In light of the fact that obviously this minister has the interest of banks and financial institutions first on his agenda and consumers last, will the Prime Minister consider splitting this portfolio into two and appointing someone as consumer minister who would look out for the interests of consumers?

Mr. Speaker, the only interest that I have in listening to my hon. friend is to make sure that he does not get sufficiently exercised that he does damage to himself again.
We think he is a national asset and we want to keep him in the House of Commons. We do not want him to hurt himself.
I take very seriously my hon. friend's suggestion. In point of fact the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is also Minister of State for Agriculture and does a remarkable job in both portfolios, and I am thinking of giving him a third.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON THE GOVERNMENT OF CANADA'S PROPOSALS FOR A RENEWED CANADA-EXPENSES OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT NOT SITTING ON COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning I contacted the secretariat of the Special Joint Committee on the Government of Canada's Proposals for a Renewed Canada, and I asked them who paid the expenses of members who are not on the committee but who went to Prince Edward Island and Toronto. I was told that although these members were not members of the committee, the committee had decided in this particular instance to pay their expenses, without being authorized to do so by the House. When I asked whether, as a
October 30, 1991

member of the Bloc Quebecois, I could have the same privileges, I was told I should get in touch with the Joint Chairman of the Committee, Mrs. Dobbie, and that each case would be examined on its own merits.
Mr. Speaker, I have two questions of privilege. One is about the different classes of members we have here: those who are members of the committee and those members in this House who are entitled to follow the proceedings of the committee outside Ottawa, outside the precincts of Parliament, and have their transportation expenses, hotel bills, meals and sundry items all paid for. Other members who, like members the Bloc Quebecois, have a different ideology, would have to submit a request for approval by a steering committee of a committee of this House, with a majority government membership, which, I imagine, would judge our case according to our political ideology and perhaps also according to sex, age or any other consideration.
Mr. Speaker, I think a very important privilege and principle is at stake here. My role in this House and in committees of the House of Commons, including the Special Joint Committee, should in no way be dictated or appear to be dictated or influenced by the arbitrary rules of a steering committee controlled by this government.
In this connection, I would ask the Chair and the House of Commons to condemn this practice by the Special Joint Committee and prohibit this entirely arbitrary process, and decide that only members sitting on the committee, or their lawfully appointed replacements, are entitled to the committee's travel expenses. Or otherwise, that all members of this House, without exception, and without being subject to arbitrary decisions, should be allowed to be on these committees and take advantage of free travel. It should also be stated that all members are equal and have the same privileges and should never have to submit to the arbitrary decisions of a steering committee in an administrative matter like this.
Mr. Speaker, this brings me to the second part of my question of privilege which also involves points of order but is nevertheless a question of privilege. It concerns the legitimacy of expenses thus incurred by the Special Joint Committee on the Government of Canada's proposals for a renewed Canada. The committee, established on June 19, 1991 in this House, by a resolution of this House-you will recall the circumstances-cannot pay the expenses of members who are not members of
Privilege
the committee or replacements on this Special Joint Committee.
On September 24, 1991, the list of members was tabled. Further to a question of privilege that I raised the next day, the Chair ruled on September 27,1991, that the NDP was entitled to only one member on that committee, Mr. Nystrom, who had been appointed, and that the other two members had not been appointed legally and were to be removed from that list until the NDP provided the Clerk of the House with the names of two members who had the right to be there, and any substitutes for them. The NDP never followed up this ruling the Speaker made on September 27, 1991. Since then, the four members who had been previously designated by the NDP, illegally, continued to sit-which they have the right to do, I agree-but at least three of them also went to Prince Edward Island, all expenses paid from Canadian public funds, with no authorization of any kind given for that purpose. I think that is completely unjust and arbitrary.
Mr. Speaker, in these extremely difficult times for all Canadians, our constituents in Quebec are shocked by such waste of public money. Mr. Speaker, much stricter control must be shown in administering public funds. I ask that the work of the Special Joint Committee be suspended until these administrative and financial issues have been clarified. I ask the Chair to see whether the funds of the House of Commons were actually used to pay the expenses of members who were not entitled to it. You know very well, Mr. Speaker, as I do, and members have always known that it is a well-established principle in Canada that no member can receive money or services from the government or the House of Commons, except his salaiy which is already provided for, without a special order of the House or a ministerial order. I think that hon. members who accepted travel advances may have unintentionally put themselves-it is not a matter of honesty or dishonesty here-in an illegal situation. It could even affect their ability to sit in this House. Nevertheless, a decision must also be made as to who shall refund to the House of Commons these amounts the committee did not have the authority to pay out and how.
I would ask the Chair to consider very carefully the allegations I just made, based on information obtained from the very members of that committee and from the

October 30, 1991
Privilege
deputy clerk of the committee because I am literally flabbergasted.
Mr. Speaker, as you may recall, we from the Bloc Quebecois had requested to sit on this committee. The participation of the Parti Quebecois was not allowed because of its ideology. I suppose that funding will now be denied to the Canadian Economic Council now that it has spoken out for sovereignty-association. This kind of partisanship that does not have its place in the House of Commons.
In closing I will say to you that I feel my privileges, as a Member of Parliament, have been breached, that such incident will never cast a doubt over my commitment to independence in the minds of the people of Megantic- Compton-Stanstead and that any unauthorized expenses will have to be reimbursed. Mr. Speaker, you probably remember that we from the Bloc-

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON THE GOVERNMENT OF CANADA'S PROPOSALS FOR A RENEWED CANADA-EXPENSES OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT NOT SITTING ON COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief in terms of commenting on some of the points made by the hon. member.
The hon. member seems to be objecting to the fact that he is not on this committee and that he, as a member of Parliament, being an equal of any other member of Parliament has the right to be on that committee. Carrying that to its logical conclusion, the only committee we can have around here is a 294 member committee, committee of the whole.
That is not the way we operate, of course. We have the recognition of the complexity of certain issues and the need to deal with many issues at the same time.
We have had for decades and decades, going back I do not know how long, the practice of assigning to committees special subjects for study. Of course, that is exactly what happened in terms of the constitutional papers and the special committee. In this case, a joint committee was set up.
Membership was established based on numerous precedents going back many years. It was dealt with no differently than any other committee. The hon. member seems to say that because he is a member of Parliament, equal to the others-we agree-that he should have his
travel expenses picked up if he chooses to travel with a committee.
Again, taking that to its logical extension, Mr. Speaker, any time a committee of this House were to travel to another country, for example, as happens frequently in terms of the studies they undertake, then every other member of the House has the right to go along.
I humbly suggest that would make it impossible for us to do anything. What is happening with the unity committee is precisely the same kind of thing that has happened in regard to committees of this House going back long before any of us were here and long before any of us were born.
There is no precedent being established here. It is established practice and I do not think the member's question of privilege has any basis.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON THE GOVERNMENT OF CANADA'S PROPOSALS FOR A RENEWED CANADA-EXPENSES OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT NOT SITTING ON COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in ruling after ruling after ruling, yourself and other Speakers before you have determined that these kinds of interventions, although it is probably appropriate that they be heard, are matters which really are properly dealt with by the committee itself.
Certainly whatever arrangements the committee has arrived at in order to do its job properly, the committee has arrived at in the context of its own authority and this is not properly a matter for the House to consider as indeed so many other Speakers, including yourself, have ruled over the years.
The committee is its own master in this respect and it is not appropriate to be debating the arrangements that have been made in the committee on the floor of the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON THE GOVERNMENT OF CANADA'S PROPOSALS FOR A RENEWED CANADA-EXPENSES OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT NOT SITTING ON COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak on this issue, even more so after hearing my colleague from Winnipeg Transcona.
The basic issue raised by the hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead is whether members of this House who are not official members of the Joint Committee on the Constitution had their travel expenses refunded or not. We claim that New Democratic members who are not officially on the Joint Committee travelled with it at the expense of the House of Commons.
October 30, 1991

Mr. Speaker, other members, including the member for	Megantic-Compton-Stanstead, would have
wanted to go with the Joint Committee across the country but did not and could not have access to travel funds.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I will go further than that. I think and I was told-I would like you to check these allegations-that the New Democratic caucus even tried to use a subterfuge by having its own members go as researchers, in contravention of the rules of this House. If that is so, Mr. Speaker, you know as well as I that they would be violating not only the practices but also the laws of this country.
The hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead thus raises a very serious matter. Mr. Speaker, all members of this House know that special provisions are required for a member to accept a cheque other than those to which he is entitled. An order in council is required for all members to go and represent a minister at the opening of a social housing project. I remember that practice, Mr. Speaker, and it took an order in council.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, for the sake of the integrity and openness of this House, we ask whether any New Democratic members had their expenses refunded and whether they acted legally. If not, Mr. Speaker, we ask you to take strong measures immediately.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON THE GOVERNMENT OF CANADA'S PROPOSALS FOR A RENEWED CANADA-EXPENSES OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT NOT SITTING ON COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, very briefly, I think that the minister who spoke earlier, the House leader, totally missed the boat. His comments were not related to the two questions asked.
I rise because I am one of those who wrote to the co-chairs of that Committee last week, to ask them precisely the question asked today by the hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead. I asked myself that question because I wanted to be involved and I was told, "Well no, Mr. Gauthier, you are not a member of the group. The six Liberal members have been appointed." So, I asked for the list of New democratic members, and I was told, "There are many of them but there is only one official member. The others take turns on the committee, on a regular basis." I asked, "Who pays for the travel expenses of these members?" and I was told, "I don't know."
I want to get an answer to those questions because it is important to know who is paying for this. While it is true
Point of Order
that committees are autonomous, it is also true, Mr. Speaker, that these committees must administer public funds in accordance with the strict guidelines of the Board of Internal Economy of the House of Commons, which ensures that those funds are spent properly.
So, the first question is: Who paid and why was this money spent on trips, hotels, and other expenses made by people who are not members of a committee? The second question is: On what authority did the Committee base its decision to spend on that? Again, I would like to receive an answer by letter or here in this House, to satisfy the curiosity of an hon. member who also wanted to participate in those meetings but cannot because the Standing Orders do not allow it.
I believe that these questions are appropriate. The question is clear and I think that the government missed the boat. I would like to get an answer.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON THE GOVERNMENT OF CANADA'S PROPOSALS FOR A RENEWED CANADA-EXPENSES OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT NOT SITTING ON COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I listened with some concern to the statements by the hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead, the Government House Leader, the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona and, of course, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier.
Generally speaking, since the complaint has to do with the proceedings of a committee, this is not a problem that should be submitted to the Chair. However, in view of the circumstances and especially after having listened to those statements, it is probably appropriate for the Chair to consider these interventions or complaints, and it might be possible afterwards to give an opinion.
As I said, it is basically a problem that concerns the committee. However, in the circumstances, it may be that the problem has a wider scope. I would ask the hon. members to give me some time to take this under advisement and then to report to the House soon.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask you if the Standing Orders allow the following. In the proceedings of the House of Commons for October 25, 1991, following Oral Questions, during Routine Proceedings, the Parliamentary Secretary to the

October 30,1991
Point of Order
Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons moved, and I quote:
That seven members and two staffers from the Standing Committee on Transport be authorized to travel to Europe from October 30 to November 9, 1991 to complete a study on high speed trains.
The hon. member for Shefford opposed this motion, Mr. Speaker, and the government House leader simply answered, and I quote:
Madam Speaker, if the Bloc Quebecois chooses to prevent this committee from proceeding on that travel, then I have no choice but to accept that at this point.
Mr. Speaker, barely ten minutes later, while my colleague from Shefford and myself had gone out for a few moments, the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Ati-kokan, seconded by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, moved to give unanimous consent to this motion authorizing seven members of this House, that is four Conservatives, two Liberals and the mover, the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan himself, to travel to Europe at the expense of the Canadian taxpayers.
Sixty thousand!

Some $60,000 will be spent, Mr. Speaker.
My question is this: we were against this motion and the government House leader accepted the Bloc Quebecois position. Just minutes later, in our absence, the motion was brought back and passed surreptitiously with the consent of the three parties. Mr. Speaker, is it normal procedure to bring back a motion during the same sitting when opposition to it has been expressed?

Mr. Speaker, I can somewhat sympathize with the concern of the member that the House had made one decision and because there was not unanimous consent, the same issue was raised later that day and there was unanimous consent given.
Now, the Bloc is not a party of the House. One of the things the legitimate parties in this House have always done to make sure that the government or any individual party does not run roughshod over the House is to make sure we have a roster of people who are in the House.
Therefore, we find it is an obligation in our caucus to make sure that we have members here at all times, so that if the government gets up and introduces a motion
that requires unanimous consent, which we do not agree to, we are indeed here doing our duty in the House and able to express our disagreement.
I believe that if any group in the House feels that they want to be involved in an ongoing basis, they should follow a similar practice.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
As Government House Leader, the Minister has full responsibility for the ordering of government business in the House of Commons. Included in this overall responsibility are the supervision of replies to written questions and the process involved in replying to such questions.
In 1975, the then Leader of the Government in the House of Commons requested that, for a period of sue weeks, the cost of answering questions be provided to estimate the cost of producing government information through the parliamentary system.
The cost accounting system used (logging of time spent and salary of each individual) proved to be time consuming, unreliable and created delays in the process of answering questions as it was too elaborate and personal. The study produced an average cost of $60 per respondent. Some questions may have up to 120 respondents (all Departments, Agencies and Crown Corporations).
With the result, the government could estimate the approximate cost of producing government information for a Session or any period of time.
Ex.: 275 questions assigned to 625 Departments, Agencies and Crown Corporations 625 respondents X $60. = $37,500 (1975 cost)
Since then, only rough estimates have been released:
1979-$100. per respondent 1981-$125. per respondent
1986-$175. per respondent
Last spring, the Parliamentary Returns Division (PRD) of the Office of the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons was requested to set up a cost accounting system to identify time consuming questions
and determine their cost while minimizing the time and cost of the exercise.
Based on the 1975 experience, it was decided that respondents would only provide the approximate total number of hours/minutes spent to prepare each response. The total number of hours/minutes includes the approximate time spent on all preparation steps i.e.: assignment, research, preparation, editing, coordinating, typing, computer time, review, translation, approval, printing, etc.
The cost of answering is arrived by multiplying the total number of hours/minutes by the average hourly rate of the Public Service plus printing cost, if voluminous. The time to calculate the cost of answering a question takes only a few seconds.
The question as enumerated by the parliamentary secretary has been answered.
